meta.title: Files & Media
meta.summary: Photos and videos don’t belong in your database — where they go instead, and how they get there and back.

goals.text: Bytes in object storage, metadata in the database
Direct uploads with presigned URLs; big files in parts
Processing, CDN delivery and adaptive video
Keeping metadata and files in step
Storage classes, lifecycle and private buckets

steps.title: Photos in the database
steps.body:
The PhotoShare app from *Napkin Math* started simply: an uploaded photo is saved as a [[BLOB]] — a binary column — right next to its caption, owner and date. One database, one backup, one place to look.

For the first few thousand users it works perfectly well.

callout.text: A photo is a few megabytes; the facts about it — owner, size, caption, when — are a few hundred bytes. They are very different kinds of data.

steps.title: Two terabytes a day
steps.body:
Now a million photos a day arrive at 2 MB each: **2 TB a day**, 730 TB in a year. The database, its replicas and its backups all grow by that much. A restore takes days, and every new replica has to copy everything.

Every photo view also travels through the app servers and the database. Images push the useful rows out of the database’s memory, and queries for captions and likes slow down.

callout.text: Databases are built to search and update small records. Shipping megabytes in and out is expensive work that only gets in the way.

changes: - Photo views crowd out everything else

steps.title: Bytes in object storage, facts in the database
steps.body:
Move the bytes to [[object storage]] — Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage. It is a huge key → file store: `PUT` a file under a key like `photos/9f2c.jpg`, `GET` it back. No queries, no joins — and no practical size limit.

It copies every object across several data centres for you and costs far less per terabyte than database disks. The database keeps one small row per photo: its key, owner, size and type.

callout.text: This split — metadata in a database, bytes in object storage — is how almost every product stores files, from profile pictures to multi-gigabyte videos.

changes: ~ Database keeps one ~1 KB row per photo
~ Database growth 2 TB → 1 GB a day

steps.title: Case: a 2 GB video over a phone connection
steps.body:
Uploads still flow *through* the app servers on their way to storage. A 2 GB video from a phone takes minutes, and the whole time it holds a server connection and memory open — just to pass bytes along.

The app servers end up sized for bandwidth rather than for the logic they actually run, and a burst of video uploads slows everyone’s page loads.

callout.text: If your servers only relay bytes they don’t look at, they are an expensive middle-man.

changes: - Each upload holds an app server for minutes

steps.title: Upload straight to storage
steps.body:
Instead, the app hands out permission and gets out of the way. The phone asks “may I upload a 2 GB video?”; the app checks the user, writes a `pending` row, and replies with a [[presigned URL]]: a link signed with the app’s key that allows *one* upload, to *one* key, for the next 15 minutes.

The phone sends the bytes directly to object storage. When the upload finishes, storage sends an event and the app marks the row `uploaded`.

callout.text: The signature can also pin the content type and a maximum size, so the URL can’t be reused to dump anything else into your bucket.

steps.title: Big files: upload in parts
steps.body:
One 2 GB request over a phone network rarely makes it in one piece. A [[multipart upload]] splits the file into parts — say 10 MB each — sent in parallel, each with its own presigned URL.

A part that fails is simply sent again; a dropped connection resumes from the last part that arrived. When every part is in, one final call stitches them into a single object.

callout.text: Parallel parts are also faster: several connections fill a link better than one. Remove abandoned, half-finished uploads automatically, or you pay to store their parts.

changes: + Failed parts retried on their own
+ Uploads resume after a dropped connection

steps.title: Make the versions people actually download
steps.body:
An original is rarely what you show. Each “upload complete” event goes onto a queue (see *Message Queues*), and workers make what the app needs: thumbnails and two or three sizes of each photo, a scan for malware, and — before anything is shared — removal of the GPS location hidden in the photo’s metadata.

Videos are transcoded into several resolutions. When a worker finishes, it saves the new files and marks the row `ready`; until then the app shows “processing…”.

callout.text: Never trust an upload. Check the real file type, size and content in the workers, not just what the client claimed.

steps.title: Serve them from the edge
steps.body:
Downloads far outnumber uploads, so they must not come through the app either. Photos are served by a **CDN** (see *Content Delivery*) with object storage as its origin: the first viewer in a city pulls a copy to the nearest edge, everyone after gets it from there.

Give each version a key that changes when its content does — `photos/9f2c_w640.webp` — and it can be cached for a year without ever going stale.

callout.text: For private photos, the app hands out short-lived signed CDN URLs — the same idea as presigned uploads, in the other direction.

changes: + CDN in front of object storage
~ Views served from the nearest edge

steps.title: Video: let the player choose
steps.body:
A video file is too big to download before playing, and viewers’ connections vary from second to second. So each video is cut into segments of a few seconds, encoded at several qualities — 240p up to 1080p — with a small playlist file listing them all.

The player fetches segment by segment from the CDN and picks the quality for the next one from how fast the last one arrived. A train enters a tunnel: the picture drops to 360p instead of freezing. This is [[adaptive bitrate streaming]] (HLS or DASH).

callout.text: Small, separately cacheable segments are also what makes video work so well on CDNs: every popular segment ends up at every edge.

changes: + Player switches quality segment by segment

steps.title: Case: rows without files, files without rows
steps.body:
Two stores can disagree. A phone gets its presigned URL and then loses signal: the row says `pending` for ever. A user deletes a photo: the row goes, but the files stay — still costing money, and still reachable by anyone who kept the link.

Fix it like any two-system update (see *Sagas*): every row has a **status**; storage events move it forward; deletes remove the row first and queue the file deletions; and a nightly **cleanup job** clears `pending` rows older than a day and files that no row points to.

callout.text: Deleting user data is a legal duty in many places. Make sure deletion reaches every copy: sizes, transcodes, backups and the CDN.

changes: + Status on every row: pending → uploaded → ready
+ Deletes: row first, then queued file deletes

steps.title: Old files can live somewhere cheaper
steps.body:
Most photos are looked at in their first few weeks and hardly ever again. Object stores sell **storage classes**: standard for hot data, “infrequent access” for less, and archive tiers that cost a fraction as much — but charge more, or take minutes to hours, to read.

A [[lifecycle rule]] moves objects automatically: originals older than 90 days go to an archive tier, while the small sizes people still browse stay hot.

callout.text: Cheap storage with expensive reads is a trap for data you still read often. Check how your files are actually accessed before archiving them.

changes: ~ Storage bill after one year $16,800 → ≈ $6,300 / month

steps.title: Case: the bucket anyone can list
steps.body:
A developer makes the bucket public “to get images showing”. Months later someone discovers they can **list** it — and download every photo ever uploaded, including private ones and the originals with their location data. Leaks like this are among the most common cloud breaches.

Keep buckets private and block public access at the account level. Serve through the CDN with signed URLs, give each service a key that can touch only its own paths, and use unguessable object names as a last line, not the only one.

callout.text: A random key is not access control. If a URL is all it takes to read a private file, that URL must expire.

changes: + Public access blocked, CDN with signed URLs

steps.title: Recap
steps.body:
• **Bytes** in object storage, **metadata** in the database — joined by the object’s key.
• Clients upload **directly** with presigned URLs; big files go in **parts** that can be retried and resumed.
• **Workers** make thumbnails, sizes and transcodes — and strip what shouldn’t be shared.
• Serve through a **CDN** with versioned keys; stream video in **adaptive** segments.
• Keep rows and files **in step**, move old files to **cheaper classes**, and keep buckets **private**.

callout.text: That completes Data & Storage. Next module: **Communication** — how services talk to each other.
